one_liner: Padding-free fp16 BERT encoder inference on NVIDIA GPUs; first-party A100 numbers show about 2x over PyTorch and 1.8x over FasterTransformer at long, variable lengths.
what_it_does: Runs one standard BERT encoder layer (QKV projection, multi-head attention, output projection, add-bias+LayerNorm, GELU feed-forward) per call on variable-length batches, using a dense [batch, seq, seq] attention mask to find the real tokens. The C++ API is a BertTransformer<OperationType::HALF|FP32> class: construct with max batch, heads, head size and max length, initialize() with device pointers to the layer weights, size a scratch buffer with cal_bufsize(), then infer() with input, mask, output, buffer, cuBLAS handle and stream; you loop over layers yourself. A TorchScript op, torch.ops.ByteTransformer.BertTransformer(...), wraps the same layer for PyTorch. Only the standard BERT encoder is supported.
how_it_is_fast: Padding-free execution: a single-block parallel prefix sum over the mask builds per-token offsets (batch_idx/word_idx), the input is packed to the valid tokens, and every GEMM and elementwise kernel runs on that packed row count; the last add-bias+LayerNorm kernel scatters results back to the padded layout. Attention is chosen by length: a single-kernel tensor-core (WMMA) fused MHA holding Q, K/V and the logits in shared memory for sequences up to 80, a split 'long' fused kernel up to about 384, and on A100 a CUTLASS-based attention for 384 < seq <= 1024 (the paper describes it as grouped-GEMM fused MHA). Other operators are fused too: GEMM with bias+GELU epilogue and add-bias+residual+LayerNorm in one pass.
when_to_use: fp16 inference of BERT-base/large-style encoders (head size 64, GELU, post-LayerNorm) on an A100 with batches of 3 or more variable-length sequences, where padding waste is large.

Batch 16 with max lengths of 448 to 1024 and average length around 60% of max: the README shows the biggest gap there (e.g. seq 512: 9.22 ms vs 13.79 for FasterTransformer with remove-padding, 21.0 for PyTorch).
A C++/CUDA inference server that wants a small per-layer encoder API taking raw device pointers, a cuBLAS handle and a stream.
Studying or vendoring a padding-free plus fused-MHA implementation under Apache-2.0.
when_not_to_use: Anything other than the BERT encoder: no decoder, GPT/LLM, T5 or training/backward pass (README: only the standard BERT encoder; issue #5 asking about training is unanswered).

Hopper, Ada or other GPUs newer than sm86: the code turns fused attention off above seq 128 when arch > 86 and uses the CUTLASS long-sequence path only on sm80; the README lists only V100, T4 and A100 and tests CUDA 11.6.
Batch size 1 or 2: padding removal is switched off when max_batch_size <= 2, and at batch 1 FasterTransformer is faster for seq 192-384 per the README.
Batch 16 at seq 64 or 256-384, where the README shows FasterTransformer with remove-padding ahead (e.g. 5.49 vs 6.85 ms at 256).
Sequences longer than 1024 tokens (the PyTorch op rejects them with 'Input seq_len too long').

integration.form: shared lib (libbytetransformer.so, plus optional TorchScript op library libths_bytetransformer.so built with -DBUILD_THS=ON)
integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit (README: 11.6), cuBLAS, cuBLASLt (Torch op), CUTLASS (git submodule 3rdparty/cutlass), PyTorch >= 1.8 for the Python plugin
integration.platforms: Linux, NVIDIA compute capability 7.0 (V100), 7.5 (T4), 8.0 (A100); data type fixed at build time (-DDataType=FP16 or FP32)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the PyTorch op builds a fresh encoder object per call and runs on the current CUDA stream and cuBLAS handle
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the TorchScript op replaces one BERT encoder layer given raw weight tensors and a dense mask; it is not a drop-in for PyTorch/Hugging Face modules or for FasterTransformer's API

gotchas: BertTransformer::bert_infer creates two cudaEvents on every call and never destroys them (src/bert_transformer.cu), and the Torch op constructs a new encoder per layer per call, so long-running services leak; open issue #11 (Sep 2023, 'memory leak' on an RTX 3090) has no maintainer reply.

The padding-free path copies the valid-token count from device to pageable host memory every layer (cudaMemcpyAsync in build_sequence_length_padding_offset_kernelLauncher), which blocks the host once per layer.
Fused attention needs fp16 and head size 64; FP32 builds and other head sizes fall back to the unfused attention, which allocates a batch x heads x seq x seq score buffer.

The benchmark harness (unit_test/python_scripts/bert_transformer_test.py) times wall clock with timeit and no final torch.cuda.synchronize(), and bert_bench.sh only times ByteTransformer, so the README's baseline columns cannot be reproduced from the repo.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over FasterTransformer for fp16 BERT-encoder serving on A100 with batches of 3+ variable-length inputs and max lengths of 448 and up, where its README beats FT's remove-padding mode by 1.5-2x; FasterTransformer also covers decoding and beam search for translation. LightSeq (also ByteDance) also accelerates training, and FlashAttention's varlen interface is the maintained choice if you only need padding-free attention rather than a whole encoder layer.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README tables on an A100 (CUDA 11.6, PyTorch 1.13.0, fp16, 12-layer BERT-base, average length 0.6 of max): at batch 16 and max length 1024 ByteTransformer takes 24.70 ms vs 53.21 for PyTorch, 65.94 for TensorFlow, 45.22 for FasterTransformer with remove-padding and 59.96 for DeepSpeed (about 2.2x and 1.8x, derived from page data); at batch 1 it is 3.16 vs 4.2 ms (PyTorch) and 4.51 ms (FasterTransformer). Only the ByteTransformer column has a public script; the IPDPS 2023 paper (best paper award, per WebSearch snippets) reports 6.13x fused MHA over PyTorch and 55% over FasterTransformer end to end but was not opened.
status_note: Stale: 11 commits, last on 2024-03-15, no releases, and the open memory-leak issue is unanswered; Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor, but expect to patch it (event leak, sm90 dispatch) before production use on current CUDA and GPUs.
